title: Walk the house before you hire anyone
summary: A slow walk with a notepad shows what to fix, what to tell buyers, and what to leave alone.
body: Start at the curb and write what you can point at before you explain it away. Look at the roof edge, the walkway, and the front door as three separate lines. A cracked step, a gutter that spills onto the siding, and a door that scrapes are not one job called the front. Note the side of the house and what you can see from the ground. You are not calling anyone yet. You are making a list a later bid can answer without a second visit to guess what you meant.

Inside, work one room at a time with the lights on. Run each faucet, flip each switch, and open each window that should open. Write hall bath, tub faucet drips instead of bathroom needs work. Soft floors, stains, and doors that stick get their own lines. If a closet smells damp, write the closet and the smell. Then walk again in daylight. Bulbs hide scuffed sills, screens that sit crooked, and a latch you only notice when the sun hits it.

Sort every line into fix, disclose, or leave. Fix means the house needs it to work, or the problem will show in a photo. Disclose means you will say it in writing even if you do not repair it. Leave means you have decided not to spend, and you will not pretend the work was done. For a fix you cannot price, ask for a written bid in dollars that says what is included. Type that number into the proceeds calculator. A hunch you say out loud is not a number.

Keep the porch as a small example. A dead bulb is often a few dollars. A loose step may only need screws you already own, unless the wood is soft and the board has to be replaced. A scraping door may need a hinge adjustment rather than a new door. Those are three costs and maybe three people. Write them apart so you do not hire one crew for the whole entry when two lines are an afternoon. When the page is sorted, you know who to call and what you will not pay for.
steps: Walk once in daylight and once with the lights on.
Write one line per issue, with the room or the side of the house.
Mark each line fix, disclose, or leave.
Get a written bid for any fix you cannot price, and type it into the proceeds calculator.

title: Fix function before you spend on finish
summary: Repair leaks, heat, and latches before you buy paint.
body: Stop the things that fail before you buy finish. A leak, a system that will not heat or cool, a loose step, and a dead outlet come before paint. A fresh coat on a damp wall does not hold, and a visitor will try the door that does not latch. Make the function list on paper and do not shop for paint until that list is done or you have a written plan for each line.

Work from water outward. If a faucet drips or a supply line weeps, shut it down and fix that joint before you touch the wall around it. A small plumbing repair can be a washer or a supply line, often a few dollars to about $20 at a hardware store if you are comfortable doing it. If the leak is inside a wall, stop and get a written cause before you close it up. Painting over a wet spot hides the stain for a short time and leaves the repair for the next person to find.

Then test what people touch on a first visit. Run the disposal or the drain and see if it clears. Run the garage door and confirm it reverses when it meets an object. Shake the handrail. Flip the outlet where a lamp would sit. These are small, and they are the tests a visitor actually does. A sticking latch is often a strike plate and two screws. A wobbling rail may be a bracket. Write the ones that fail and fix those before you talk about floors.

If a heater, a cooler, or a water heater is near the end of its life, get that in writing from the person who looked at it. Then decide whether you will repair it or describe it in your disclosure. Do not hide a tired system behind a rug or a fresh wall. The invoice, or the note that you will disclose it, goes in the same folder as the function list. Paint and floors are the last lines, and only after the function list is checked off.
steps: Stop active leaks before you buy paint.
Test drains, the garage door, handrails, and the outlets a lamp would use.
Get a failing system in writing, then repair it or plan to disclose it.
Plan paint and floors only after the function list is done.

title: Clear surfaces before you add anything
summary: Empty counters and floors do more for a showing than extra decor.
body: Pack until each room has one job: sleeping, cooking, eating, or sitting. Buyers are trying to see the floor, the counters, and the walls. Extra decor on top of a full counter makes that harder, not easier. Clear first. Add nothing until the room already reads as that one job.

On a kitchen counter, leave one or two useful things: a kettle you use, or a board, not a crowd of jars. A clear stretch of counter photographs as work space. Do the same on a dresser and a desk. In the bath, leave the soap you are using and put the rest in a bin under the sink. Floors get the same rule. Pull chairs, baskets, and small tables off the walking path. If two people cannot pass without turning sideways, one piece leaves the room.

Store packed boxes outside the photo frame. A dining room full of bins reads as storage, even if the table is pretty. The garage, a closet you will not open, or a room you will not photograph can hold the boxes for now. Label them by the room they came from so you are not opening every box on a showing morning. A roll of tape and a marker are the whole kit.

If you still want one added piece, make it useful and singular. A lamp that works on a side table is enough. A made bed is enough. Do not buy a tray, a new vase, and a set of pillows to solve a room you have not cleared. Those extras are often $20 to $60 you do not need, and they land on the surfaces you just emptied. Walk the path you want photographed and take one more thing off each surface before you call it done.
steps: Give each room one job and clear it to that job.
Leave one or two useful items on a counter, and pull furniture off the walking path.
Keep packed boxes out of the rooms you will photograph.
Add nothing new until the cleared room already works.

title: Pack personal items before the first showing
summary: Box photos, mail, and papers so the rooms show the house.
body: Box personal photos, mail, and papers before the first photographer or visitor. Those objects pull the eye off the room and onto your life. A frame on a mantle, a stack of mail by the door, and a calendar full of names are three boxes, not one vague tidy-up. Do this while you still have a week, not the hour before the appointment.

Start with paper. Tax folders, medical notes, and anything with an account number go in a box that rides with you later, not on the truck in a random stack. Mail comes off the counter and out of the basket by the door. Take names, notes, and calendars off the refrigerator. Wipe the door so the outline of a magnet is not the new focal point. A single clear fridge door does more than a new bowl of fruit.

Collections are the same job. If a shelf of figures or a wall of plates is the first thing someone sees, box enough that the shelf and the wall show. You do not have to empty the house of everything you love. You do have to keep the camera from stopping on it. Close closets you do not want opened, and do not overstuff the ones you leave. A closet that will not shut is an invitation.

If you still live there, pick one cupboard for daily items and keep the rest clear on showing days. The path from the front door through the main rooms should not dodge a backpack, a pair of shoes, or a project on the floor. Walk that path the night before and again in the morning. Anything that blocks it moves, even if you use it every day. Put it in the one cupboard or in the car.
steps: Box photos, mail, and papers before the first visit.
Clear the refrigerator door and wipe it.
Leave closets you will not show shut, without overstuffing the ones that stay open.
Walk from the front door to the back and move anything in the path.

title: Price the property you have
summary: Compare sold homes that match this property, then write the net you will accept.
body: Pull recent sold listings, not the ones still asking. A sold price is a closed number. An active price is a wish. Match this house on facts you can check: bedroom count, bathrooms, size, lot, garage, age, and the updates the listing actually described. Three sold homes you can describe beat ten you only glanced at. Write the address or the listing id, the sold date, and the sold price on one row each.

Then adjust for condition you can point at. If a sold house had a new roof and yours does not, say so in a line under that row. If yours has a garage and that one did not, say that too. Do not add a story about what a buyer might feel. If you cannot see the difference in the photos or at the property, do not invent a dollar gap. Drop a sale you cannot describe. It is not a match.

Write three numbers before you pick a list price: the price you will advertise, the net you hope to clear, and the lowest net you will accept. The lowest net goes into the proceeds calculator with your payoff and your costs, not with a round number you hope is close. Run the calculator once at the advertised price and once at a lower price so you can see the net move. The gap between those nets is the room you have for a later credit.

Keep this page with the offer notes. When someone suggests a list price, you can set it next to the three sold rows and the bottom net. If the suggestion ignores a difference you wrote down, ask about that difference before you agree. You can change the price later. You should not pick the first number without the sold rows and the net you already said you would accept.
steps: Compare at least three sold properties and write the date and price for each.
Adjust only for condition you can point to, and drop a sale you cannot describe.
Write the advertised price, the net you hope for, and the lowest net you will accept.
Run the proceeds calculator at the list price and at a lower price before the first offer.

title: Leave room to answer a real offer
summary: Set the list price with room for a credit and still hit your net.
body: The list price is the number on the ad. The net is the decision. If you set the list price at the exact dollar you need to walk away with, the first repair credit puts you under your line. Price, credits, and timing move together. Write the list price on one line and the net you need on the next, and do not let those two numbers become the same sentence.

Decide in advance which givebacks you can live with. A repair credit, a closing-cost credit, and a later closing date are three different flexes. Pick two you will talk about and one you will not. A move-out date you have already booked may be the one you will not trade. Write that down while you are calm, before a caller is waiting. You can change the page later. You should not invent it on the phone.

Run a plain example on the calculator. Take the list price, subtract a credit of a few thousand dollars you might actually offer, and read the net. Then try a smaller credit. The point is not a magic figure. The point is that you have seen the net move before anyone asks. If the larger credit drops you under the walk-away net, that credit is not one of the two you can flex. Say so on the page.

Recalculate every time a real credit changes. A counter that feels close is not close until the proceeds line matches the net you wrote. Keep the flex list with the calculator printout. When you answer, you are choosing among terms you already priced, not discovering your limit out loud. If none of the flexes save the net, the answer is a different price or a no, and both of those can be written in one sentence.
steps: Keep the list price and the net you need on two separate lines.
Pick two terms you can flex on and one you will not.
Run a sample credit through the calculator before anyone asks.
Recalculate proceeds every time a real credit changes.

title: Take listing photos in daylight with the lights on
summary: Open the shades, turn on the lamps, and keep the camera level.
body: The camera needs more light than your eyes do. Open the window coverings and turn on the overhead lights and the lamps you are leaving before you frame a shot. Shoot when you can see the corners of the room. If a corner falls black, add the lamp or wait. Do not hope the listing page will brighten it. A dark corner is where people assume the room stops.

Glare on bare glass can wash a wall out. If the sun is hitting that window, wait for it to move or shoot the room from a different corner. Do not close only one shade to fight the glare if the rest of the house is open. Clean the glass you will shoot through first. Streaks show up once the light is even. A bottle of glass cleaner is a few dollars, and it belongs in the photo kit with the cloth.

Stand in a corner and keep the camera level. If the walls lean in the frame, the room looks smaller than it is. Use a doorway as the level check: the trim should run straight up the side of the photo. Take one wide photo and one detail photo in each main room, then stop. Extra tilted frames do not give you a better wide shot. They give you a pile to delete.

Before you leave a room, close toilet lids, move the trash can out of the frame, and coil a hose if it sits in the front photo. Turn the lights on even in the daytime. A lamp that is off reads as a dead lamp. If a bulb is out, replace it before the appointment. A bulb is a few dollars, and a dark fixture in an otherwise bright room is the thing people notice. Check the front of the house from the sidewalk with the entry light on if you are shooting late in the day.
steps: Clean the windows you will shoot through and open the coverings.
Turn on the lights before you frame the shot.
Keep the camera level and take one wide photo and one detail in each main room.
Move trash, close lids, and replace a dead bulb before you call the set done.

title: Photograph the work you finished
summary: Give finished repairs their own clear photo, and lead with the front of the house.
body: People scroll quickly. A clear photo of a repaired step, a new faucet, or the label on a replaced water heater answers a question before the showing. Give each finished repair its own frame, with enough light to read the work. Do not bury it in a wide shot where the repair is a speck. If you cannot tell what was fixed, the photo is not done.

Do not feature a project you have not finished. An open wall, a missing fixture, or a taped joint belongs in the disclosure conversation, not as the first image. If the work is half done, finish it or leave it out of the set and say so in writing. A photo of an unfinished repair invites a credit request you have not priced. The repair folder should hold the invoice next to the photo so you can show what was done and when.

Lead the set with the best daylight photo of the front. Then the kitchen, each bathroom, and the main living space, before the extra rooms. A buyer who never gets past the first five images should still have seen the front and the rooms they will use every day. Retake any shot where the repair is blurry or dark. A soft photo of a new faucet is worse than no photo, because it looks like you are hiding the finish.

Keep the repair set short. One photo per finished item is enough. Name the file by the room and the item so you can find it when someone asks. If a repair is behind a panel, photograph the label or the access panel with the door open and the light on. You are not decorating the set. You are answering the question a careful visitor will ask with a picture you already took.
steps: Put the best daylight photo of the front first.
Include one clear photo of the kitchen, each bathroom, and the main living space.
Give each finished repair its own lit frame, and leave unfinished work out.
Retake any repair shot that is blurry or dark, and keep the invoice with the photo.

title: List the jobs before you pick who does them
summary: Write every job in a sale, then decide who will do it and what it costs you.
body: Hiring an agent and selling it yourself are two ways to cover the same work. The jobs do not disappear because you picked a path. Write them down: pricing, photos, showings, disclosure forms, offer review, negotiation, and closing coordination. One line each. Next to each line, write the name of the person who will do it and what it will cost you in hours or dollars.

Use your own rates in the commission comparison. This site does not fill in a rate for you. If you do not know an agent's fee, leave the dollar cell blank and ask for it in writing before you compare. A blank is allowed. A made-up percent is not a plan. Hours count too. A showing you will host is an hour cell, not a free cell. Add those hours so the money column is not the only cost.

If you sell it yourself, you can still offer to pay a buyer's agent. That choice is a line you enter. It is not a requirement and it is not a default. Write yes or no, and if yes, write the amount you would offer so it can go in the calculator. Do not leave it as we will see. The same is true of photos. If you will hire a photographer, ask the fee and put it on the line. A photo fee of a few hundred dollars is a real cost next to a commission, and it belongs on the page before you order a sign.

Ask any agent you interview for a written list of what they will do, and set it beside your list. Gaps are the jobs you would still own. Decide who owns each job before you order a sign or book photos. If a line has no name, you are not ready to advertise. The sign can wait a day. A missing owner on offer review cannot.
steps: Make two columns: the job, and who owns it, with hours or dollars.
Leave a fee blank until you have it in writing, and enter your own numbers in the calculator.
Decide whether you will offer to pay a buyer's agent, and write the amount or a no.
Ask any agent you interview for a written list before you order a sign.

title: Questions to answer if you sell it yourself
summary: Forms, showings, and offer review are still yours if you sell without an agent.
body: Selling without an agent does not remove the forms, the showings, or the offer review. It assigns them to you. Start with the forms. Ask a local real-estate attorney or the closing company which seller disclosures your state expects. This site cannot tell you. Write the form names and where to get them. Do that before you advertise, because a missing page is slower to fix after a buyer asks.

Then decide the showing path in sentences you can keep. How does a buyer book a time. Where will you be during the visit. What gets put away first. Set hours you can actually keep for the next few weeks, and write them down. If you cannot be there, write who locks up. A plan you cannot perform is not a plan. Share the hours before the first call so you are not inventing them while someone is in the driveway.

Plan the offer path before the first contract arrives. Who receives it. Who reads it with you. How quickly you will answer. Have an attorney or an agent review the first contract before you sign it, and ask what that review costs before you need it at night. The fee is whatever they quote you. Put the phone number on the same card as the showing hours. A contract you sign because you did not know who to call is an expensive way to save a call.

Read those three answers out loud: forms, showings, offer review. If one of them is still someone will handle it, stop and name the person. You can still hire help for a single job. You should not start showings with the offer path blank. The questions are the work. Answering them on paper is how you find out whether you are ready to sell it yourself.
steps: Ask a closing company or attorney which seller forms apply, and write the list.
Write showing hours you can keep, and who locks up.
Name who receives the first contract and who reads it with you.
Have an attorney or agent review that contract before you sign it.

title: Read the whole offer before you answer the price
summary: Credits, dates, and contingencies change the money more than the headline price.
body: Find the purchase price, the seller credits, the earnest money, the financing terms, and every date before you react to the price. Credits, dates, and contingencies change the money more than the headline. Read with a pen. Highlight every dollar that leaves your side and every deadline. If a number is in an addendum and not on the first page, it still counts. The first page is not the offer.

A higher price with a large credit can leave you with less than a lower price with no credit. Type both sets into the proceeds calculator before you reply. Use your payoff and the costs you already listed. Write the two nets under the two headlines. The better-looking price may lose. Do this even when you like the buyer. Liking the buyer is not a line on the statement.

A repair request is a request. It is not a promise you already made. List what you will do, what you will credit, and what you will decline. If the request has no dollar amount, do not answer yes. Ask for the amount or get a bid, then rerun the net. Ask your agent or attorney what each contingency lets the buyer do, and write that answer in the margin. A word you do not understand is a reason to ask, not a reason to sign.

Check the expiration before you finish the reading. If the offer dies tonight, you still read the credits first. A fast yes to a number you did not run is more expensive than a written request for another day, if the form allows you to ask. Save a copy of what you received, with your highlights, in the offer file. The reply you send later should match the margins, not a version of the deal you remember.
steps: Highlight every dollar that leaves your side and every deadline, including addenda.
Run the high price with its credit and the lower price without one through the calculator.
List what you will repair, credit, or decline, and ask what each contingency allows.
Save the marked copy in the offer file before you answer.

title: Compare net and dates before you counter
summary: Put each offer on one row and counter the gap in your net.
body: Make one row per offer before you counter anything. The columns are the price, the credits, the closing date, and what has to happen first, such as an inspection, an appraisal, or a loan approval. A row that is missing a date is not ready to compare. Go back to the offer and fill it in. If two offers arrive the same day, they still get two rows. Do not merge them into a blend.

Run the proceeds calculator for each row and write the net in the last column. Use the same payoff and the same costs on every row so the difference is the offer, not a change in your assumptions. A date you cannot move on is a no even when the net is higher. Circle the row that meets the net you wrote down and a timeline you can actually meet. If none do, the counter is the specific gap: the credit, the date, or the net. Write that gap in plain numbers.

Answer before the offer expires. If you need more time, ask for it in writing. Do not let a deadline pass in silence if you still want that offer. Silence is an answer you may not mean. Put the expiration time at the top of the row so you see it before you refine the wording. A counter that arrives late is a new offer, and you should not assume the other terms survived.

Recalculate after every counter, including your own. A concession you add in the last sentence can drop the net under your line. Read the row out loud once before you send it: net, date, and what still has to happen. Send the answer in writing the way the form requires, and file the row with the copy. If a third offer shows up, it gets a row too. You do not throw out the page because the stack got thicker.
steps: Build one comparison row per offer, with price, credits, date, and what has to happen first.
Calculate the net on each row with the same payoff and costs.
Counter the specific gap, or ask for more time in writing before the deadline.
Recalculate after every counter and send the answer in writing.

title: Build the closing folder before you have a buyer
summary: Collect payoff contacts, receipts, and a wire-check plan before you are under contract.
body: Start the folder before you have a buyer. Paper or digital, pick one home for it and do not split the documents across a counter and an inbox. Label each piece: payoff contact, association contact if you have one, warranty paperwork you plan to transfer, and receipts for repairs you are disclosing. A folder you can hand to someone is the point. A search through email is not a folder.

Keep the disclosure draft in that folder and update it when a repair is finished. The version you sign should match the house on signing day. When you replace a page, date it and pull the old page out so you do not sign the stale one. The repair invoices sit behind the draft. If a buyer asks what you fixed, you are holding the answer instead of promising to send it later.

Ask the closing company how they send wire instructions, and write that answer in the folder. Plan to confirm any wiring instructions by calling a phone number you look up yourself, not a number that arrived only in an email. Read the amount and the account name back. This is a phone call, not a courtesy. Do it before you send money, including an earnest-money wire if that money is yours to send.

When you have a contract and a closing date, request the payoff and put the quote in the folder with the good-through date. A payoff that expires before closing needs a refresh. Set a reminder a few days ahead. The same folder should hold the inclusion list, the photo of the finished repairs, and the utility card once you make it. One home means that on closing morning you pick up one thing, not five.
steps: Give the folder one home and label the payoff contact, warranties, and repair receipts.
Update the disclosure draft when a repair is finished and remove the stale page.
Call a number you look up yourself to confirm wiring instructions before you send money.
Request the payoff when you have a contract and a closing date, and note when the quote expires.

title: Walk the house again before the buyer’s final visit
summary: Check the fixtures you promised to leave, and report anything that broke.
body: Use the same room list you used for showings and walk it again before the buyer's final visit. Test the lights, the appliances you are leaving, and the faucets. Replace bulbs that are out. A bulb is a few dollars, and a dark fixture at the walkthrough becomes a debate you could have skipped. The walk is easier when you have already done the tests they are about to do.

Read the inclusion list while you walk, not after. The contract says what stays. Do not remove a fixture, a rod, or an appliance you agreed to leave. If you are taking something, it should already be on the goes list and it should be gone or clearly labeled before they arrive. Remove trash, leftover paint, and hardware you are not including. A can of paint in the garage reads as a project you did not finish.

If something broke after you signed, tell the buyer in writing before they find it. A note the day before is easier to solve than a surprise at the walkthrough. Say what broke, whether you will repair it or credit it, and the amount if you know it. Rerun the net if the answer is money. Do not wait in the hallway to explain a leak you discovered yesterday.

Do a last pass for personal papers in drawers, including the kitchen and the office. Leave remotes, keys, codes, and garage openers where the contract says they go. If the contract is silent, put them in one labeled envelope on the counter and mention it in the note. Walk out and come back in through the front door once. Anything you would not want found in the next hour gets resolved now, on paper or in the truck, not during their visit.
steps: Walk the same room list and test the lights, appliances, and faucets you are leaving.
Check the inclusion list in each room and do not remove an item you agreed to leave.
Report anything that broke, in writing, before the visit.
Leave remotes, keys, and codes where the contract says, and clear personal papers from the drawers.

title: Book the move after the closing date is real
summary: Wait for a contract date, then book the truck with a written backup plan.
body: A target date can move. Put a deposit on a mover or a truck when the closing date is in the contract, and not before, unless the cancellation terms are cheap and written down. Confirm the date with the closing company before you pay. Then ask what happens if that date shifts by a day or two. Get the answer in writing: the fee, the notice they want, and whether the truck is still available.

Measure sofas, mattresses, and tables that might not fit through the next door before the truck is in the driveway. Write the numbers and share them with the mover, or use them yourself if you are loading. A piece that will not pass should be sold, left, or routed through a different door now. The ramp is a bad place to decide. If the written estimate excludes stairs or a long carry, ask what those cost and add the figure to the move budget on your net page.

If you are packing yourself, start with rooms you do not use every day. Keep a first-night box in your car: chargers, a change of clothes, basic tools, and anything you need before the truck is unpacked. That box does not go on the truck. Label it and put it in the seat, not in the garage where it can be loaded by mistake. The closing folder rides in the same car.

Read the cancellation line again the week of closing. If the date slips, you already know the phone number and the fee. Call before the window closes. A move booked on a real contract date, with a written backup and a box that stays with you, survives a one-day shift. A move booked on a hope, with your papers on the truck, does not.
steps: Confirm the closing date with the closing company before you book.
Get the mover's cancellation terms in writing, including a shift of a day or two.
Measure the large pieces and price any carry the estimate leaves out.
Pack a first-night box and keep it with you, along with the closing folder.

title: Label boxes by the room they go to
summary: Name the room on two sides of every box and keep a first-night box with you.
body: Write the room and a short contents line on every box. Kitchen, pans is enough. Bedroom, linens is enough. Write it on two sides so a stack does not hide the label. A label on the top only disappears as soon as another box lands on it. Use a thick marker. A pen looks neat in the kitchen and vanishes in the truck.

Number the boxes and keep a simple list on paper or on your phone. Box 14, kitchen, pans. When a box is missing, the number tells you what to ask about. The list rides with you, not in box 14. Update it when you add a box, not at the end of the day when you are guessing. A list you trust is the whole system. A list you stopped keeping is decoration.

Carry documents, spare keys, and the closing folder in the car. Do not put them on the truck. Jewelry and any small thing you cannot replace go in the same car. The truck is for boxes you can wait a day to open. Load the first-night box last so it comes off first, and keep it out of the truck entirely if there is room in the car. First off only works if nobody stacks a mattress on it.

At the new place, call the room as you unload and check the number off the list. A box marked kitchen that arrives in the garage is still a win if the list says it arrived. Do not retape labels at the destination unless a label tore. The name you wrote at the old house is the name on the list. Finish the check-off before you start unpacking, so a missing number is obvious while the truck is still there.
steps: Label at least two sides of each box with the room and a short contents line.
Number the boxes and keep the list with you.
Carry documents, keys, and the closing folder in the car, not on the truck.
Check the numbers off as you unload, before the truck leaves.

title: Replace cracked caulk before photo day
summary: Cracked caulk shows up in close photos. Replace it while the repair list is still short.
body: Walk the wet joints with the lights on before photo day. Look along the tub, the shower, the kitchen sink, and the backsplash where the counter meets the wall. Cracked or missing caulk reads as a leak in a close photo even when the wall behind it is dry. Put each joint on one line: sound, cracked, or missing. You only recaulk the lines that fail.

Pull the old bead out instead of smearing new caulk over it. A plastic scraper or an old card lifts most of it. Wipe the joint and let it dry. If the gap is still damp the next morning, you do not have a caulk job. You have a leak, and it belongs on the function list. Soft drywall or a stain that keeps returning is the same stop. Do not photograph a fresh bead over a wet wall.

Lay a thin line, not a thick smear. Tape both edges if your hand wanders, run the bead, then smooth it with a damp finger and pull the tape. A tube of kitchen and bath caulk is often under $10, and a tube is enough for a tub and a sink if you are not filling a wide gap. A thick ridge photographs as a repair. A thin line photographs as a finished joint. Let it cure before anyone runs that shower.

When the joint is dry, take one close photo for the repair folder and one wider photo the way the listing will show the room. If the old caulk was stained but the new line is clean, you do not need a new surround. If the pan or the tile is soft, stop and price that repair before you spend the afternoon on a bead. Write the finished joints on the photo list so you remember to shoot them in daylight.
steps: Check every wet joint with the lights on and mark the ones that are cracked or missing.
Remove the old bead and let the joint dry before you recaulk.
Lay a thin line, and stop if the wall behind it is soft.
Photograph the finished joint for the repair folder.

title: Finish the entry before the rest of the house
summary: The front door and entry are the first rooms a visitor stands in. Finish those before the back closets.
body: The front door is the first room a visitor stands in. Finish it before you reorganize a back closet. Wash the door, the glass, and the hardware. If the handle is loose, tighten it. If it is broken, replace that piece. A single handle set is often about $20 to $60 at a hardware store, which is a different job from refinishing the whole door. Make sure the house numbers can be read from the street. A set of numbers is often under $20. A visitor who cannot find the house is already late.

Open and close the storm door or the screen if you have one. A stuck closer or a torn screen is an afternoon, not a remodel. A storm-door closer is often about $15 to $30. Adjust it so the door shuts on its own and latches. Then check the entry light. Replace a dead bulb, and confirm the switch by the door actually controls that light. People arrive in the evening. A dark step is a function problem, not a style problem.

Clear shoes, mail, and coats down to what you use this week. One mat and a working light are enough. A plain mat is often $15 to $40. Extra benches and a pile of shoes make the entry look smaller than it is. If the floor is the first thing in the photo, sweep it after you have moved the pile, not before. The pile sheds.

If you only have one day before photos, spend it on the entry, the kitchen counters, and the main bathroom. Leave the deep closet for another day. The order matters because the first thirty seconds happen at the door. Before every showing, not only before the photo shoot, do the same five-minute pass: clear the mat, turn on the light, and shut the closet. Write that pass on the showing list so it is not a memory.
steps: Clean the door, tighten or replace the hardware, and make the house numbers readable.
Fix a stuck storm door and confirm the entry light works.
Leave one mat, and clear the daily pile.
Repeat that clear-out before every showing, not only before photos.

title: Write your bottom line before the first showing
summary: Write the lowest net you will accept, and do it before anyone asks.
body: Open the proceeds calculator and type your payoff, the commissions you expect to pay, closing costs, credits, and repairs. The result is a draft of your net, not a promise.
Write the lowest net you will accept on paper and put it with your offer checklist. Change it only when a real number in the deal changes.
When an offer arrives, you already know which gaps matter. You will not have to invent a bottom line while someone waits on the phone.
steps: Enter your own costs in the calculator.
Write the lowest acceptable net where you can find it.
Update it when the payoff or a credit changes, not when you feel rushed.

title: Keep the camera level and skip the distortion
summary: A tilted wide shot makes a straight room look small. Keep the camera level.
body: Hold the phone or camera at about chest height and level with the floor. If you tilt up, the ceiling takes over the photo. If you tilt down, the floor does.
Step back before you zoom with your feet. Extreme wide angles bow straight lines. A buyer who visits will notice that the room does not match the picture.
Take two frames of each room and keep the one where the door casing is vertical. Delete the other so it does not end up in the listing by mistake.
steps: Use a level line in the room, such as a door frame, to check the camera.
Shoot from a corner, not from the middle of the room.
Keep the frame that matches what a person sees when they walk in.

title: Put every deadline on one page
summary: Every offer has dates. Put them on one page so none expire in silence.
body: Copy each date out of the contract onto one page: offer expiration, earnest-money due date, inspection end, appraisal, loan commitment, and closing.
Add the name of the person who has to act. A date with no owner is easy to miss.
Check the page every morning while you are under contract. If a date is close and you are not ready, call your agent, attorney, or the closing company that day.
steps: Transfer dates the hour you receive an offer or a counter.
Name an owner for each date.
Look at the page before you agree to a new credit or a new closing day.

title: Call the closing office before you wire
summary: Look up the closing office and call them before you send a wire.
body: Wire instructions that arrive by email can be altered. Treat a last-minute change of bank details as a stop sign.

Look up the closing company’s phone number on its own site or on the paperwork you received at the start, then call. Read the routing number and account number back. Do not use a phone number that was only in the email.
If anything does not match, do not send the wire. Ask the closing officer to reissue the instructions in the way they normally do.
steps: Save the closing company’s main phone number when you open the file.
Call that number and read the wire details back.
Refuse rushed changes that you cannot confirm on the phone.

title: Deep-clean after the dusty work, not before
summary: Clean after the dusty repairs, not before. Archived because the prep tips now cover the order of work.
body: Sanding, patching, and caulk throw dust. If you deep-clean first, you will clean again after the last repair.
Do the messy jobs, let the dust settle, then clean top to bottom: lights and trim, then counters, then floors. Save the floor for last so you are not tracking grit back across it.
This note stays in the archive so the order is still written down. The active prep tips now carry the same sequence: function first, finish next, clean before photos.
steps: Finish dusty repairs before the deep clean.
Clean from the top of the room toward the floor.
Schedule photos after the floors are dry.

title: Test the alarms before you list
summary: Press each smoke and carbon-monoxide alarm, and replace any battery that fails.
body: Walk the house and press the test button on every smoke alarm and every carbon-monoxide alarm you can find. Count them as you go: hall, each bedroom, the kitchen if there is one there, and the basement. A unit that stays silent needs attention before a showing. A unit that chirps every minute will chirp during the visit, and that sound is what people remember.

If the test is weak or the unit chirps, replace the battery before you replace the whole alarm. Buy the battery size printed on the old one. A pack of the common sizes is often under $15 at a hardware store. Put the used batteries in the bag you take back out, so you do not leave them on a counter that will be in a photo. Test the unit again after the new battery is in. A fresh battery that still produces silence means the unit itself should be replaced.

A hallway alarm that chirps only at night is the usual example. It has been low for days, and the quiet afternoon test is how you catch it before a buyer does. Write the date you tested on a card in the closing folder. If a unit is past the date printed inside the cover, replacement is the honest fix. A new alarm is often in the $15 to $40 range, depending on whether it also detects carbon monoxide. Read the package and mount it where the old one was, unless the old spot was a dead corner with no air.

Do not take the batteries out to stop a chirp and then forget them. An alarm with no battery is not a fix. After you list, test again the week of the first showings. Ten minutes with a chair or a short ladder covers most houses. The chair stays in the garage when you are done, not in the hall photo.
steps: Press the test button on every smoke and carbon-monoxide alarm.
Replace a weak battery with the size printed on the unit.
Replace the unit if a fresh battery still produces silence, or if the printed date has passed.
Test again the week of the first showings.

title: Clear the gutters before showings
summary: Empty the gutters and check that downspouts send water away from the foundation.
body: Look along the roof edge on a dry day, from the ground and from a stable ladder if you are comfortable using one. Leaves and grit in a gutter spill over the siding in the next rain, and that streak shows up in the front photo. Write which run is full: front, back, or a side. You do not need to clean a gutter that is already empty.

Scoop the debris into a bucket, not onto the bed below if you can help it. Gloves are enough for a light season. A small gutter scoop is often under $15 if your hands will not fit. Work from the downspout back toward the high end so you are not pushing a pile into the outlet. Bag the debris with the rest of the yard waste when you are done.

Then prove the water moves. Run a hose at the high end and watch. Water should travel to the downspout and land several feet from the wall. If it pours over the front lip, the gutter is still clogged or it is pitched the wrong way. If it pools at the foundation, add an extension. A plastic downspout extension is often about $10 to $20. Aim it so the water does not dump onto the walk someone will use.

Write the result on the repair list before you buy paint for the siding. A clean gutter does not fix a seam that leaks or a spike that has pulled out. Those are separate lines, and a handyman bid for a rehang is a number you can compare with the paint. If you will not get on a ladder, hire the cleaning and ask for a note that says the downspouts ran. Do this before showings, and again after a heavy drop of leaves if the house sits under trees.
steps: Scoop leaves and grit from the gutters that are actually full.
Run a hose at the high end and watch where the water lands.
Add a downspout extension if water sits by the wall.
Write any leak or loose hanger on the repair list before you paint.

title: Tighten loose hardware before the first visit
summary: Snug the hinges, handles, and cabinet pulls that rattle when someone opens a door.
body: Open every door and drawer once, including the garage, the hall closet, and the cabinet under the sink. A loose hinge or a wobbly pull shows up the moment someone tries the house. It is also one of the cheaper fixes on a prep list. A screwdriver you already own, plus a small bag of wood screws, is often the whole shopping trip. At a hardware store that bag is commonly a few dollars, and a mixed pack of hinge screws is often under $15.

Work one room at a time so you do not lose track. Open the door, lift the handle, and see if the screw turns. If it snugs up and the pull stops rattling, you are done with that piece. If the screw spins in the hole and never tightens, the hole is stripped. Move the screw a little, or use a slightly longer screw of the same thickness so the threads bite fresh wood. Do not keep cranking a spinning screw. It will not hold, and the hole gets worse.

A kitchen is a clear example. Cabinet doors next to the stove get opened all day, and the top hinge is often the loose one. Tighten that hinge, then the pull, then move to the next door. On a bedroom door, check the strike plate if the door does not latch. Two screws there, snug but not cranked until the wood splits, usually fix a door that bounces open. If the plate is bent, a replacement plate is a few dollars and the screws that come with it are the right length.

Skip a new set of pulls unless a piece is broken or missing. Matching hardware for a whole kitchen can run from about $40 for simple pulls to well over $100 if you replace every door and drawer. That money does not make a loose hinge latch. Function comes first. After you finish, walk the same path with the lights on and open each door once more. Anything that still moves goes back on the list.
steps: Open every door and drawer, including the garage.
Tighten screws that move, and replace a spinning screw with a slightly longer one.
Replace only pieces that are broken.
Open each door once more before you call the job done.

title: Trace a stain to its source
summary: Find the leak that made the stain, then repair that before you paint over the mark.
body: A ceiling spot or a bubbled patch of paint means water was there. Painting the mark hides it for a week and then the spot returns, often larger. Mark each stain on the walk-through list with the room and whether it is on the ceiling, the wall, or the floor. One mark per stain. Do not group them into the house has a few spots.

Look for the source before you open a can of paint. Above a ceiling stain, check the bath or the supply line on the floor over it, then the roof if there is no room above. At a wall, check the window above the spot and the pipe in that bay. Press the surface. Soft drywall or a hollow sound means the water was not a one-time drip you can cover. If you cannot find the source, hire someone who can and ask them to write the cause, not only the price.

Repair and dry the source first. A supply line under a sink is often a hardware-store part, from a few dollars for a washer to about $20 for a braided line, if that is truly the leak. A roof or a hidden pipe is a bid. Save the invoice with your other receipts so you can tell a buyer what was fixed, when, and by whom. The invoice is the sentence you will wish you had if someone asks about the patch.

Only then patch and paint the stain. Match the sheen you already have so the patch does not flash in a photo. If the source is repaired and dry, one photo of the finished ceiling is enough for the folder. If you decide not to repair it, the stain stays on the disclose list in plain words: where it is, and that you do not know the cause or that you do. Do not describe a painted spot as a finished repair.
steps: Mark each stain on the walk-through list with the room and the surface.
Find the leak, or get the cause in writing, before you paint.
Repair and dry the source, and save the invoice.
Patch only after the source is dry, or disclose the stain instead.

title: Run the heat and the cooling before showings
summary: Turn each system on, listen for a short cycle, and change a dirty filter.
body: Turn the heat on and wait. Stand at a supply vent until the air is actually warm, not merely until the thermostat clicks. Write the time it took and whether every vent you can reach did the same. A system that blows cold at one room and warm at another is a line on the repair list, not a story you tell at the showing.

If the house has cooling, switch to it after the heat test and wait again until a vent is cool. Do not run both claims on the same minute. Listen for a short cycle: the blower starts, stops, and starts again before the room has changed. A short cycle can be a clogged filter. Slide the old filter out, read the size printed on the frame, and write that size down. A common one-inch filter is often about $10 to $30 depending on the size. Write the size on the new frame or on a card in the closing folder so the next change is not a guess.

Replace the filter before photo day if it is grey and packed. A clean filter does not fix a system that will not start. If the heat or the cooling refuses to run, stop and put that on the repair list before you schedule photos. A quiet system is easier to explain than a dead one, and a technician's written note is what you want in the folder. Ask what they found and what it will cost before you approve the work.

On showing day, set the temperature to something ordinary and leave it. Do not shut the system off to hide a noise. If a bedroom vent is closed, open it so the room is not stale. Check the condensate line or the pan if you know where it is and you have seen a drip there before. A small drip goes on the function list. Do not wipe it and hope. The test you already wrote down is the one you repeat the morning of the first visit.
steps: Run the heat until a vent is warm, and note any room that stays cold.
Run the cooling until a vent is cool, if the house has it.
Replace a dirty filter and write the size down.
Put any system that will not start on the repair list before photo day.

title: Leave a clear path through each room
summary: Move chairs and baskets so a visitor can walk in, turn around, and see the floor.
body: Walk from the front door to the back of the house the way a stranger would. Every time you turn sideways, stop. A chair in a doorway, a bin in a hall, or a cord across a rug is a path problem. The fix is to move the object, not to explain it. A buyer who is watching their feet is not seeing the room.

Start with the widest walk you can make without buying furniture. Pull dining chairs in. Slide a bench out of the entry. Coil a lamp cord along the baseboard. If a rug slides, a short roll of rug tape is often under $15, or you can roll the rug up for showing days and store it in a closet. Bare floor that you can walk is better than a rug that bunches.

Use the path from the kitchen to the back door as the example. If a trash can, a dog bed, or a stack of shoes sits in that line, move all of it for showings. The shoes go in a closet. The bed goes in the spot you chose for pet gear. Then walk the path again with your hands at your sides. If an elbow hits a cabinet or a chair, the path is still tight.

You do not need to empty the house. A made bed, a table that fits, and a chair you can sit in can stay. What leaves the path is anything that makes a person step around it. On showing mornings, the same walk takes five minutes if the extra pieces already have a home. Give them that home before the first appointment, not during it.
steps: Walk from the front door to the back and stop wherever you turn sideways.
Move chairs, bins, and cords out of that line.
Tape a sliding rug or roll it up for showings.
Walk the path again with your hands at your sides.

title: Open the window coverings the same way
summary: Raise every shade to the same height so the light looks even from room to room.
body: Walk the house and set each shade, blind, or curtain the same way before you take a photo or open the door. One closed room beside a bright one looks accidental, and it makes the dark room look smaller. Pick one height you can repeat: shades just above the midpoint, or fully up. Write it on a card by the door so the morning of a showing is not a new decision.

Work room by room, including the ones down the hall. A blind that hangs crooked is worse than no blind. If a covering is broken, take it down for showings rather than leaving it slumped. A bare, clean window is easier to read. Replacing a single vinyl blind is often about $15 to $40 if you want it back up before photos. Measure the width inside the frame before you buy, and write the inches on the list so you do not come home with the wrong one.

Open the coverings before you turn the camera on, and look for glare. If a bare window washes the wall out, shoot that room from the other corner or wait until the sun moves. Do not close one shade to fight the glare and leave the others up. The set should still match. Dust the sill while the covering is open. A bright sill full of grit shows up once the light is even.

Do this again the morning of a showing. It takes a few minutes, and it is one of the first things people notice when they look from the doorway into the next room. If you live in the house, the bedrooms will have been closed overnight. The card by the door is the reminder. Check the street-facing windows last, from the sidewalk, so the front of the house matches the rooms inside.
steps: Pick one height and set every covering to it.
Remove a covering that will not hang straight, or replace it after you measure.
Look for glare and dust the sills while the windows are open.
Check the coverings again the morning of a showing, including from the sidewalk.

title: Put pet gear away before showings
summary: Move bowls, beds, and litter out of sight, and air the rooms they sat in.
body: Pet gear tells a visitor about the animal, not about the room. Before a showing or a photo appointment, pick up bowls, beds, toys, leashes, and the mat by the door. Put them in one closet or in the garage, somewhere you can find them again the same day. The room should show the floor, the window, and the way through.

A water bowl by the back door is the usual example. It leaves a ring, and it sits in the path. Move the bowl, wipe the ring, and check the corner for a toy that rolled under a chair. Litter boxes should be scooped and, for the hours of the showing, moved to a closed laundry or bath that is not on the photo list. If that is not possible, clean the box and close the door of that room only if you are also willing to have the room skipped. Do not pretend a closed door hides a smell.

The cost is time and a rag. Budget fifteen to thirty minutes before each showing if the animals live in the main rooms. A small bin or one laundry basket makes the pickup faster the second time. You are not redecorating. You are clearing the things that only make sense to the household.

When the showing is over, put the bowls back before you do anything else so the animals are not waiting on an empty kitchen. If you have more than one showing in a day, leave the basket by the closet. The reset should be the same each time, not a new plan invented at the door.
steps: Pick up bowls, beds, toys, and leashes before a showing.
Wipe the spot where a bowl sat.
Move a litter box only to a room you are willing to have closed or cleaned.
Put the gear back as soon as the showing ends.

title: Stop after one simple table setting
summary: A plain setting on the table is enough. Extra decor on every surface works against you.
body: A dining table needs to look like a table, not like a shop display. Set one place for each person who actually lives there, or set none at all if the table is small. A plate, a glass, and a napkin are enough. Stop there. Extra candlesticks, a runner plus a centerpiece plus folded napkins in every glass make the room look arranged and hide the table itself.

You do not need to buy a new set for photos. Use what you already own. If the everyday dishes are chipped, choose the four that are not, and leave the rest in the cabinet. A plain tablecloth you already have can cover a worn top. A new cloth, if you want one, is often $15 to $40. That is optional. The clear table is the point, not the linen.

Look at the chairs next. If a chair blocks the walk from the kitchen to the living room, pull it in or move it out for the showing. An example: six chairs around a table that seats four makes the room feel tight. Two of those chairs can live in a bedroom for the week you are showing the house. Count the path, not the matching set.

On photo day, set the table last, after the counters are clear, so you are not walking dishes back through a finished room. Then leave it. Adding one more object is how a simple setting becomes a pile. If you still eat there between showings, clear the meal and reset the same simple places. The reset should take five minutes.
steps: Set only the places you actually use, or leave the table clear.
Use dishes you already own.
Move extra chairs that block the walk through the room.
Reset the same simple places after a meal.

title: Leave closets partly empty
summary: Take out enough clothes and boxes that a visitor can see the rod and the floor.
body: A closet packed to the ceiling hides the storage you are selling. Open each closet you will leave unlocked and look at the rod and the floor. If you cannot see both, it is too full. You do not need an empty closet. Half full reads as usable. The goal is a gap, not a staging trick.

Box what you will not wear during the weeks of showings. Out-of-season clothes and extra linens can live in a labeled bin in the garage or in a closet you will keep shut. Leave a gap on the rod about the width of a jacket, and a clear patch of floor you could set a pair of shoes on. Do the same for a linen shelf: a few folded stacks, not a wall of towels. If a shelf is bowed, that is a repair line, not a folding problem.

Do this in the coat closet, the bedroom closets you will open, and the utility closet if the water heater or the panel is in there. People look. A utility closet with a path to the panel is more useful than one stuffed with bags. Slide stored paint and loose hardware into one bin so the floor is visible. Keep chemicals upright and closed. You are not hiding the closet. You are letting someone see its size.

Check the doors after you remove the bulk. A door that would not latch because of the pile should latch now. If it still will not, the latch belongs on the function list. On photo day, shoot one closet only if it is genuinely easy to read. A dark, jammed closet is better left shut than featured. The morning of a showing, open the ones you planned to show and confirm the gap is still there.
steps: Open each closet you will leave unlocked and find the rod and the floor.
Box what you will not use during showings and leave a gap.
Fold linen into a few stacks, and clear a path in a utility closet.
Confirm the door latches, and only photograph a closet you can read clearly.

title: Write three numbers before you list
summary: Write the list price, the net you hope for, and the net that would make you walk away.
body: Before you talk with an agent or a buyer, write three numbers on one page. The first is a price you might list. The second is the net you hope to clear at that price. The third is the net where you would rather stay put. Those numbers are yours. A conversation is easier when the page already exists.

Use the proceeds calculator with figures you choose. Run it at the price you might list, and run it again at a lower price you would still consider. Write both nets under the prices. Include the payoff and the costs you already know. If you do not know a cost, leave a blank and go find it. A blank is more honest than a zero you typed to make the page look finished.

The walk-away net is the useful one. It is not a wish and it is not a dare. It is the line under which you stop and rethink the sale. Circle it. If a later offer, after credits, lands above that line and on a date you can meet, you have a real decision. If it lands below, you are not required to talk yourself into it because the headline price looked familiar.

Keep the page with your offer notes, not in a message thread. After any pricing talk, add a line: the price discussed, the net you calculated, and what you agreed to do next. If a later conversation drifts, you can read what you already decided. Update the three numbers when a real bid or a real payoff changes them. Do not update them because a conversation was enthusiastic.
steps: Run the calculator at two prices you might list.
Write the net you hope for and the net where you would stop.
Leave a blank for any cost you do not know yet.
Keep that page with your offer notes and update it when a real number changes.

title: List credits before you pick a price
summary: Write the repairs and concessions you already expect, then see what they do to your net.
body: A list price that ignores a likely credit is a guess. Before you choose the number on the ad, write the credits you already expect. That might be a repair you know about, a closing cost you are willing to cover, or a credit for something you will not fix. One line each, with a dollar amount you did not round into the air.

Get the amounts from something you can point at. A written repair bid is better than a feeling that the deck will cost something. If you have no bid yet, write a placeholder and label it as a placeholder, then replace it when the bid arrives. Type the real amounts into the calculator as seller credits or repairs. The net that remains is closer to a decision than the list price alone.

Read that net before you fall in love with a list price. If the credits you already expect push the net under your walk-away number, the list price is too low or the credit is too large. Change one of them on purpose. Do not discover this after you have told someone the price. The order is credits, then net, then the number you advertise.

You can change the list later. You cannot change it wisely if the credits were never written down. When an offer arrives with its own credit, set it next to the credit you already expected. If the offer's credit is the one you planned for, you are comparing like with like. If it is a new item, add a line and rerun the net before you answer. Keep the credit list on the same page as the three numbers.
steps: Write the credits you already expect, each with an amount.
Mark any amount that is still a placeholder until a bid arrives.
Enter the credits in the calculator and read the net.
Choose the list price only after that net is one you can accept.

title: Match what was included in a sold home
summary: Before you compare a sold price, write what that sale included and what yours includes.
body: Two houses can close at different prices because one included the appliances, a repair credit, or a roof, and the other did not. The headline price does not say which. Before you treat a sold price as a match for yours, write what that sale included and what yours includes. If you cannot find those facts, that sale is not a comparison. Drop it.

For each sold home, make one row: the date, the sold price, and the items the listing said were included or credited. Look for appliances, a closing credit, and repairs the seller agreed to finish. Then make the same row for your house. A refrigerator you plan to take is a difference. A water heater you replaced is a difference. Write both in plain words. Do not convert them into a mood.

Use only sales you can describe this way. Three thin rows you understand are more useful than a long list of prices. If the listing is silent on what stayed, do not guess that it matched yours. Silence is a reason to drop the sale, not a reason to assume the best. Ask your agent, if you have one, to pull the concession line from the closed file when that line is available to them. If it is not available, say so on the row.

When you set your list price, read your row next to theirs. If your house is missing something theirs included, your price should reflect that on purpose, or your credit list should. If yours includes something theirs did not, that belongs in the photo set and in the inclusion list, not only in your head. Attach this page to the pricing notes so the first offer is compared with the same facts.
steps: Pick sold homes that are similar on facts you can check.
Write what each sale included or credited, and write the same items for your house.
Drop a sale you cannot describe.
Use those rows when you set the list price and when you read the first offer.

title: Rerun the net after each repair bid
summary: When a written bid arrives, put that number in the calculator before you agree to the work.
body: A bid is a fact. A guess about what the work will cost is not. When a written bid arrives, type that number into repair costs on the calculator before you agree to the work. Read the new net out loud and write it under the bid. If you skip this, you are approving a project without knowing what it does to the money you planned to walk away with.

Compare that net with the walk-away number you wrote before you listed. If the net falls below that line, you have three honest choices: skip the project, raise the list price on purpose, or accept a lower net and change the page. Do not do the work and hope an offer will cover it. The bid will not shrink because the kitchen looks better in a photo.

Keep the bid with the calculator printout. Later, a buyer who asks for a credit is easier to judge against a number you already accepted or refused. If you declined a $1,800 bid, you should not be surprised by an $1,800 credit request for the same item. Write on the bid whether you approved it, and the date. One page, not a text you cannot find.

Ask the bidder what is included before you type the number. A price that excludes haul-away or a permit is not the full cost. If the bid is a range, use the high end for the calculator and label it. You can be glad if the invoice comes in lower. You do not want the net to depend on the low end. Rerun the calculator again when the invoice arrives if it differs from the bid you approved.
steps: Enter the written bid as a repair cost before you agree to the work.
Compare the new net with your walk-away number.
Skip the project, change the price, or change the walk-away number on purpose.
Save the bid, what it includes, and the printout together.

title: Keep price notes in writing
summary: After each pricing talk, write the price, the net, and what you decided.
body: A phone call is easy to remember two different ways. When you finish a talk about price, write three lines before you do anything else: the price discussed, the net you calculated, and what you agreed to do next. Date the note. If you wait until evening, you will smooth the conversation into the version you prefer.

Store the note with your offer page, not only in a text thread. A thread is hard to read next to the calculator. One page in the pricing folder can hold a month of these notes, each a few lines. If a later conversation drifts, you can read what you already decided instead of debating a memory. This record is yours. It is not a promise to a buyer until you sign something that says so.

Write the net from the calculator, not from the headline. If someone said the price works, ask which costs they included and write those down. A price that works before a credit and a price that works after a credit are different notes. Label them. If you did not run the numbers during the call, say in the note that the net is still blank and run it before you agree to the next step.

At the end of the week, read the notes in order. You should be able to see whether your list price, your hoped-for net, and your walk-away net are still the ones on the original page. If a note changed one of them, update the original page and initial the change. Do not let the latest call silently replace the decision you made when you were calm. The next step you wrote is the thing you do, or the thing you cross off with a reason.
steps: Write the price, the net, and the next step after each pricing talk.
Date the note and file it with your offer papers.
Leave the net blank if you have not calculated it yet, then calculate it.
Update your three numbers only when a note actually changes them.

title: Shoot in the order a visitor walks
summary: Start at the street, then move through the house in the order someone would walk it.
body: Start at the street, then move through the house in the order someone would walk it. Take the front first, from the sidewalk if you can do that without standing in the road. Then the entry, then each main room. That order shows you a closet door left open or a light still off before you are done, and it gives you a set that tells a simple path instead of a pile of rooms.

Do not start in the prettiest bedroom because the light is good there. You will forget the front, and the front is the photo people see first. If the sidewalk view includes a car or a bin, move those before this pass, then shoot. Write the room names in walking order on a card and check them off. A missed bath is easier to see on a card than in a camera roll of forty frames.

Save detail shots for the end: a finished repair, a fireplace, a view from a window. Lead with the rooms. If you mix details into the walk, you will spend the best light on a faucet and run out of even light for the wide shots. One wide frame per room while you walk. Details after you have a wide shot you would actually use.

When you reach the back door, turn around and walk out the way you came, looking for what the first pass missed. A lamp you turned on should still be on. A shade you set should still match the others. If a room failed, reshoot it before you pack the camera. The walk order is also the order you will sort the files later, so name them as you go or sort them the same day.
steps: Photograph the front from the sidewalk before you go inside.
Move room to room in walking order and check each room off a card.
Take the wide shot while you walk, and add detail shots after.
Walk back out and reshoot any room that failed before you pack up.

title: Move cars before the photo appointment
summary: Clear the driveway and the curb in front of the house so the photo shows the property.
body: A car in the driveway hides the garage and the walk. Move vehicles off the driveway before the photographer arrives, or before you take the shots yourself. That includes a car you think is beside the frame. Look through the camera, or stand where the photo will be taken, and check the edges. A mirror or a bumper in the corner still reads as a parked car.

Plan the parking before the appointment, not when the photographer is in the street. If you need an hour somewhere else, ask a neighbor only for that hour and do not block their drive. Write down where each vehicle went so you are not hunting for keys when it is time to bring them back. Bins belong in the same pass. Roll them out of the frame, then bring them back when you are done so they are not left at the curb overnight.

Look once from the sidewalk before you shoot. The hose, a trash can, and a pile of pots count as clutter in the front photo even when the cars are gone. Coil the hose and set the can in the garage for the hour. This is a staging pass, not a cleaning day. Five minutes at the curb saves a reshoot. If you are hiring a photographer, tell them the driveway will be empty so they do not schedule around a car you forgot.

Put the cars back when the front photos are done if you need the driveway, and keep them off it if more exterior shots are coming. The same rule applies on a showing day when you expect someone to pull up. A clear drive lets them see the house they came to see. Write move the cars on the photo checklist above turn on the lights, because a lit entry behind a truck is still a photo of the truck.
steps: Move vehicles off the driveway and check the edges of the frame.
Park them where they will not block someone else's drive.
Roll bins out of the frame and coil the hose.
Look once from the sidewalk before you shoot, then bring the bins back.

title: Close lids and hide trash cans
summary: Shut toilet lids, tuck trash cans into cabinets, and clear the edge of every tub.
body: Before anyone takes a photo, walk the rooms that will be in the set and look for lids and bins. Close the toilet lid in every bathroom. Close the washer if the laundry will be photographed. A lid that is up becomes the subject of the picture, and the room behind it disappears. This takes a few minutes and costs nothing if the lids still work.

Move trash cans out of the frame. A kitchen bin beside the cabinet, a bathroom basket by the sink, and a recycling bin in the corner of a dining room all read as clutter even when they are clean. Slide them into a closet, a garage, or the space beside the refrigerator where the camera will not see them. If a bin has no lid and it smells, empty it into the outdoor cart first. A box of trash bags is a few dollars and is worth having on photo day.

Use the main bathroom as the example. Close the lid, fold the towel once, and move the wastebasket into the tub only if the tub will not be in the shot. If the tub is in the shot, the basket goes in the linen closet instead. Then stand in the doorway and look at the same corners the camera will see. If you can still see a bin, it is not hidden.

Put the bins back when the photos are done if you are still living there. Write a one-line note on the photo checklist so the same bins get moved again on showing mornings. The habit is the point. A buyer should see the room, the fixture, and the floor, not yesterday's trash.
steps: Close toilet lids and any other lids in the photo set.
Empty a bin that smells, then move cans out of the frame.
Stand in the doorway and check the corners the camera will see.
Put the bins back after the photos if you still live there.

title: Take one wide shot and one detail
summary: For each main room, keep one photo that shows the whole room and one that shows a finished feature.
body: For each main room, keep two frames and be willing to delete the rest. The wide shot shows the whole room from a corner, with the camera level, so the walls do not lean. If you cannot fit the room in one frame, step back into the doorway rather than tilting up. A tilted wide shot makes a large room look like a hallway. Take that frame before you move a lamp into a prettier spot that blocks the corner.

The detail shot is one thing you finished, closer in: a repaired window, a clear counter, a made bed. It is not a second wide shot from the other corner. Pick the feature you would mention if someone asked what you did in that room. If you did not finish anything there, skip the detail rather than photographing a random object. One honest wide shot is better than a detail of clutter.

Delete frames that repeat the same angle. A short set is easier to sort than a roll of near-duplicates, and duplicates hide the one frame that was level. On a larger screen, keep the wide shot where the corners are visible and the detail where the finished work is sharp. Name them room-wide and room-detail so you do not upload five versions of the kitchen.

Do this for the main rooms only. A hallway does not need a pair. The front of the house still leads the set, and it can have its own wide shot plus one detail of something you fixed outside, such as the step or the numbers. When a room has no clean wide shot, go back and take one. Do not promote a detail to the wide slot. People need to see the size of the room before they see the faucet.
steps: Take one level wide shot of each main room from a corner or the doorway.
Take one closer shot of something you finished, or skip the detail.
Delete frames that repeat the same angle.
Do not use a detail shot as a substitute for the wide shot.

title: Delete blurry frames the same day
summary: Review the set before you upload it, and drop any frame that is dark, tilted, or soft.
body: Review the set before you upload it, on a larger screen than the phone you shot with. A frame that looks fine on a small screen can be soft, dark, or tilted on a listing page. Do this the same day, while you can still reopen a shade and try again. Tomorrow the light will be different and you will talk yourself into keeping a bad frame.

Delete shots with a tilted line, a dark corner you did not mean, or a reflection of the person taking the photo. Soft focus on a wide shot of a main room means that room has no wide shot yet. Retake it. Do not keep a blurry frame as a backup. Backups are how the wrong photo gets uploaded. If the only front photo has a car in it, that is not a keeper either. Reshoot the front.

Name the keepers by room as you delete. Kitchen wide, kitchen sink, primary bed wide. A named set of a dozen frames is a listing. An unnamed roll of eighty is a chore you will postpone. The postpone is how a dark photo goes live. Put the keepers in one folder and the rejects in another only if you need them for a repair record. Otherwise delete the rejects so you cannot pick them by mistake.

If a room still has no clean wide shot at the end of the review, it goes back on the photo list for the next daylight, not into the upload. Tell anyone helping you which folder is the one to send. One sentence in a message, with the folder name, prevents a second person from attaching the camera roll. The same-day rule is the whole tip: sort while the house is still set the way you shot it.
steps: Review every frame on a large screen the same day.
Delete soft, dark, tilted, or reflected shots.
Retake a room if the wide shot is not clean.
Name the keepers by room and upload only that folder.

title: Price the hours you will spend
summary: Write the tasks you would take on, then estimate the hours before you decide to sell it yourself.
body: Write the tasks you would take on if you sell it yourself, each on its own line: showings, calls, form review, and offer replies. Next to each line, write the hours you can actually give it in a normal week. A showing block of two hours is not the same as being on call all day. Be specific. Tuesday and Thursday, four to six, is an hour number. Whenever they want is not.

Add the hidden hours. A call to book a showing, the time to clear the house, the time to lock up, and the time to write the answer are four lines that people fold into the showing. If you write only the visit, you will undercount. Forms have hours too. Reading a disclosure packet and filling it in is not free because you are not paying a commission on that hour.

If the hours are more than you have, that task is a reason to hire help or to pay someone for that piece only. This is a schedule, not a judgment. The commission calculator can show the money. The hour list shows the time. Put both on the table before you decide. A task you cannot staff is a task you should price out, even if the quote is simply ask a photographer or ask an attorney what a review costs.

Look at one sample week on paper. If three showings, two offer reads, and the calls already fill the hours you wrote, you do not have a spare evening for a new repair bid.
