Hire that piece out or move the list date. Redo the hour list when your week changes. The decision to sell it yourself can stay. The decision to personally do every line does not have to.
steps: List each task you would keep, including calls and lock-up time.
Write the hours you can give it in a normal week.
Hire out a task that does not fit the week.
Read the hour list next to the commission calculator before you decide.

title: Decide who answers buyer questions
summary: Name the person who will reply, and decide that replies go in writing.
body: Pick one person to answer buyer questions before you advertise the house. That person can be you, a co-owner, or the agent you hired. The point is that a caller does not get two different answers about price, showing times, or what stays. Write the person's name at the top of a sheet and keep that sheet by the phone you will actually answer.

The sheet needs the list price, the showing hours you can keep, and the two or three facts you are willing to say out loud. An example: the roof was repaired in a year you can point to on a receipt, the refrigerator stays, and offers should be sent to a named email. If you do not know a fact, the answer is that you will check and call back. Guessing a repair date on the phone is how a small question becomes a disclosure problem.

Decide what the answer person will not discuss. Price negotiation belongs in a written offer, not in a friendly call. If someone asks for your lowest number, the prepared line is that you will read a written offer. Practice that line once so it is ready. If two of you own the house, agree on that line together before the first call, and let the other person know when a call came in.

There is no fee for the sheet. The cost is the hour you spend writing it and the discipline to use it. If you hired an agent, ask them to send you the same sheet so your answers match. If you are selling it yourself, you are the answer person, and the sheet is what keeps a tired evening from inventing a new price.
steps: Name one person who answers buyer questions.
Write the price, the showing hours, and the facts you will say.
Agree on the line you will use when someone asks for your lowest price.
Log each call on the same sheet.

title: Learn which forms you must use
summary: Before you advertise, ask which seller forms your state expects and where to get them.
body: Rules vary by state. A form that worked for a friend somewhere else may not be the one you need, and a form you found online may be the wrong year. Before you advertise, ask which seller forms your state expects and where to get the current copies. A local real-estate attorney or the office that handles closings can answer that. Write the names they give you. Do not rely on memory for a list of papers.

Ask two practical questions with the list. Which pages does the seller complete. Which pages does someone else prepare. Write the answers in the margin. A disclosure you must sign is a different task from a report you only receive. If they tell you a form is required only in some cases, write the case in the margin so you do not skip it because you forgot the condition. Bring the questions in writing so the answer comes back in writing.

Do this before the listing goes live. Filling out a form after a buyer asks is slower, and it is easier to miss a page. Set aside a block of time to complete the seller pages while the house is quiet. If a question on the form does not match something you know, leave it blank and ask, rather than guessing a fact about a repair. The repair folder you already built is the place you look before you answer.

Keep a clean copy and the filled copy in the closing folder. When a page is updated because a repair finished, replace the old page and date the new one. Showings can start when the required seller pages are complete, not when you meant to finish them. If the closing office named a fee for preparing their part, write that fee on the job list so it is in the calculator before you decide you are saving every cost.
steps: Ask which seller forms your state expects, and where to get the current copies.
Write who completes each page, and any case where a form applies.
Complete the seller pages before you start showings.
File the filled set in the closing folder and replace a page when a repair changes the answer.

title: Plan showing hours before you advertise
summary: Choose the days and hours you can leave the house, and write them down before the first call.
body: Showings need an empty-enough house and someone to lock up. Pick the days and hours you can keep for the next few weeks and write them down before the first call. A window you can repeat, such as weekdays from four to six and one weekend morning, is a plan. Call us anytime is not. If you advertise hours you will not keep, the first week will be a string of apologies.

Decide how a visitor gets in, and write that next to the hours. You meet them, an agent uses a lockbox, or someone you hired stands at the door and locks up after. If a lockbox is part of the plan, ask what it costs and who controls the code before you count on it. The cost is the number they quote, not a number you invent. Write who can change the code and when the box comes off the door.

Pair the hours with the clearing routine. The entry, the counters, and the path have to be ready at the start of each window, not sometime during it. If you cannot clear the house and leave it, those hours are not real. That is a reason to hire help rather than a reason to guess. Put the clearing time inside the hour count you already wrote for the week so you do not double-book yourself.

Share the plan before the first request. Put the hours in the listing notes and on a card by your phone. When a request falls outside the window, you can say the next open time instead of inventing one. Review the card each Sunday and change it if your week changed. A plan you update is still a plan. A plan you ignore is how strangers arrive while you are in the shower.
steps: Write the days and hours you can actually offer for the next few weeks.
Decide how a visitor gets in and who locks up.
Put the clearing time inside those hours.
Share the plan before the first request, and update it when your week changes.

title: Write what you will not negotiate
summary: Before the first call, list the terms you will discuss and the ones you will not.
body: Price is not the only term that moves. Closing date, credits, and what stays with the house all move too. Before the first call, list the terms you will discuss and the ones you will not. One page, two short lists. You can change it later. You should not invent it while you are on the phone.

The will-not list should be short. One or two items is enough. A move-out date you have already booked is a clean example. A fixture you already promised to a buyer in a signed inclusion list is another. If everything is negotiable, say that, and still write the net you will not go under. A list that says nothing is negotiable is not serious. A list that says nothing is off limits will get decided by whoever talks fastest.

Read the page before you answer a caller. If they ask for the one date you will not trade, you already have the sentence. Offer a term you will discuss instead, such as a credit you already priced, if that is still true. Do not trade the fixed item because the conversation is friendly. Write the request and your answer in the offer file the same day, even when the answer is no.

After the first real offer, look at the page again. If you want to move something from one list to the other, do it in writing with the reason, not in the middle of the call. Then rerun the net if the change has a dollar figure. The page is a tool for a calm decision. It is not a script you have to follow once the facts have changed, and it is not a secret. Anyone helping you answer should have the same two lists.
steps: List the terms you will discuss and the terms you will not trade.
Keep the will-not list to one or two items, or to the net you will not go under.
Read the list before you answer a call.
Change a list only on purpose, then rerun the net if money moved.

title: Answer an offer in writing
summary: Send a written yes, no, or counter, even when you already talked it through.
body: A spoken yes is easy to remember two different ways by the next morning. After you decide, write the decision in a sentence and send it the way your forms require. The sentence should say accepted, rejected, or countered, and it should name the offer you mean, including the date on it. A text that says we are good is not that sentence.

Include the price, the credits, and the dates you are accepting or changing. If you change only the closing date, say the price is unchanged so nobody fills the silence with a different number. Leave out anything you have not decided. A maybe on the refrigerator does not belong in the counter. Finish the inclusion list first, then answer. An answer with a blank you meant to settle later is an invitation to argue.

Have the person who is reviewing the contract read the sentence before it goes, if that is the plan you wrote down. Ask them to check that the written answer matches the row on your comparison page. A counter that drifts from the row is how the net changes without a new calculation. If they mark a correction, rerun the net before you send it. Speed is not a reason to skip the row.

Save a copy in the offer file the same day, next to the offer you received. If a second offer arrives, you will want the first answer on paper so you do not accept two deals or contradict yourself. Note the time you sent it. When the other side replies, the reply goes in the same file, and the row gets updated. The conversation can be pleasant. The file is what you will have at the closing table.
steps: Write the decision in one sentence: yes, no, or counter, naming the offer.
Include price, credits, and dates, and leave out anything you have not decided.
Check the sentence against your comparison row and rerun the net if it changed.
Save a copy in the offer file the same day.

title: Split price from the closing date
summary: When you counter, change the price on one line and the closing date on another.
body: A counter that changes the price and the date in one breath is hard to compare. Write the price you want on its own line. Write the closing date you can actually meet on the next line. If you need more days to move, say that as a date, not as a feeling. Around the end of the month is not a date. The 28th is a date. Use a calendar when you pick it.

Check each line against a different page. The price line has to survive the proceeds calculator with the credits you are also offering. The date line has to survive the mover, the possession terms, and the walk-away schedule you already wrote. A higher price with a date you cannot keep is not a better offer. You would be paying for that price with a broken move.

If you can give on one line and not the other, say so. You can accept their price and counter only the date, or the reverse. Put the unchanged item in words so it does not get renegotiated by accident. Then read both lines against your net page one more time. A date that adds a week of costs you have not typed in, such as an extra mortgage payment you know you will owe, belongs in the calculator before you call the date easy.

Send the two lines in the written counter, not only in a phone call that explains them. File a copy with the comparison row. If they come back on only one line, you can answer that line without reopening the other. That is the point of splitting them. You can see which term moved. When both lines are acceptable, the acceptance should repeat both so the final paper matches the two lines you meant.
steps: Put the price on one line and the closing date on the next.
Pick a real date from a calendar, not a feeling about the month.
Check the price against your net and the date against the move.
Repeat both lines in the written counter or the acceptance.

title: List what stays before you sign
summary: Write the appliances, fixtures, and window coverings that stay, and the items you will take.
body: Offers often assume the appliances and the attached fixtures stay. If you plan to take a refrigerator, a curtain rod, a mirror, or a shelf in the garage, write that down before you sign. A list you only remember is not part of the deal. Walk the house with a pen and mark stay or goes on each item you might argue about later. Do it in daylight so you do not skip the back of the garage.

Include the rooms people forget: the laundry, the shed, the attic pull-down if a fixture is mounted there, and the yard if a bench is bolted down. Window coverings are a common miss. If the drapes stay and the rods go, say both. If a television mount stays and the television goes, say both. The more ordinary the item, the more likely someone assumes the opposite of what you meant.

Attach the list to your counter or your acceptance. Handing it over later, after the papers are signed, is how you discover it was never part of the contract. If the form has a section for inclusions and exclusions, copy your marks into that section and keep your walk list behind it in the file. Read the form's section out loud against the walk list once. An item on the walk list that never made it onto the form is not in the deal.

If you are replacing an item before closing, write the replacement on the list too. A tired washer you will swap for the one from the apartment should be described, or you should leave the one that was there. Do not swap after signing and hope nobody notices. The final walk is easier when the list, the house, and the form all name the same things. Take the goes items out before that walk, or label them so nobody thinks they were stolen.
steps: Walk the house in daylight and mark stay or goes, including the garage and the shed.
Write window coverings, rods, and mounts as their own lines.
Copy the list into the form and attach it to the paper you sign.
Remove the goes items before the final walk, or label them.

title: Ask who pays for requested repairs
summary: When a buyer asks for a repair, write the cost and who pays it before you agree.
body: A request to fix something is a money question. Before you say yes, get a bid or name a credit amount. A yes without a number is a blank check. Ask who orders the work and who pays. A credit you give at closing is different from a repair you finish before the final walk. One changes the net on the statement. The other changes your week and still might not satisfy the request if the work runs long.

Write the choice in three lines: the item, the amount, and who does the work. If you will credit $1,500 and do nothing, say that. If you will hire the plumber and pay the invoice up to a number you name, say the number. If the bid is not in yet, the written response can say you will answer when the bid arrives, if the deadline allows. Do not fill the wait with a spoken promise.

Rerun the proceeds calculator with that amount filled in before you send the answer. If the credit drops you under the walk-away net, reduce the credit, decline the item, or change your net on purpose. Compare the request with bids you already refused or accepted. You may already have a number for this exact repair in the folder. Use it. A new request does not erase the old bid.

Put the three lines in the written response and save them with the offer row. At the final walk, the house should match what you agreed to finish, and the statement should match what you agreed to credit. If a repair will not be done in time, say so before the walk, not during it. Who pays is a sentence you can write today. It is a poor surprise on the last afternoon.
steps: Get a bid or name a credit before you agree to a repair request.
Write who orders the work, who pays, and the amount.
Rerun your net with that amount, and stop if it crosses your walk-away line.
Put the choice in the written response and match the walk and the statement to it.

title: Save every counter you send
summary: Keep a copy of each counter in one folder, in the order you sent them.
body: Each counter you send is a version of the deal. Save it the day you send it, not when you remember at the end of the week. Use one folder, paper or digital, and put only sent copies in it. A draft you almost sent does not belong next to the one the other side received. Number the copies by date so the newest is obvious.

When a new version arrives, read it beside the one you sent. Highlight only the lines that changed: price, credit, closing date, or what stays. An example: if the only change is the closing date, the highlight is that date, not the whole page. You can miss a one-line change if you reread the document as if it were new. The folder is what makes the comparison possible.

A simple folder and a pen are enough. If you want a paper set, a folder is a few dollars. If you keep digital copies, name the files with the date and the word counter, and keep them in one directory for this property. Do not leave the only copy in an email thread you might archive. Save the attachment into the folder the same day.

If you have an agent, ask for the same set in your folder. If you do not, you are the file. Before you send the next counter, open the last one you saved and check that you are changing the line you mean to change. A counter that accidentally drops a credit you already accepted is an expensive kind of tidy-up.
steps: Save each counter the day you send it.
Number the copies by date.
Highlight only the lines that changed on the next version.
Open the last saved copy before you send another.

title: Read the settlement statement when it arrives
summary: Check the price, credits, and payoff on the statement the day you receive it.
body: The statement is the math of the sale. Read it the day it arrives, not in the lobby. Start with four lines: the sale price, the payoff, the credits you agreed to, and the amount you are supposed to receive. If any of those is missing, ask the closing office which page it is on before you assume the deal got simpler. A missing credit is not a gift. It may be on another page.

Compare those lines with your net page and the signed offer. Circle anything that does not match. A credit you never agreed to, a payoff that does not match the quote in your folder, or a proceeds number you cannot rebuild from the lines above it all get a circle. Do the arithmetic on paper. If you cannot get from the price to the proceeds with the lines they printed, you are not ready to sign.

Call the closing office about a mismatch before the appointment. Bring the circled page and the signed page that disagrees with it. Ask them to explain the line in a sentence you can write down, and ask for a revised statement if the line was wrong. A correction in the lobby is harder, and it is easier to initial something you do not understand when people are waiting. The phone call is the appointment that matters.

Check the prorations and the dates while you have the file open. A tax or association line should match the dates in the contract closely enough that you can see why it is that amount. If you cannot see why, circle it too. File the final statement in the closing folder when it matches, and carry that copy with you. The version on your screen the night before is not a substitute for the pages you will initial.
steps: Read the price, payoff, credits, and your proceeds the day the statement arrives.
Circle lines that do not match the contract or that you cannot rebuild.
Ask about those lines before closing day, with the signed page in hand.
Carry the matching statement to the appointment.

title: Match the move-out date to the contract
summary: Read the date you must be out, and book the move to finish before that day.
body: Find the possession line in the contract and write that date on a calendar you look at every day. The date you hoped for and the date you signed can differ by a weekend or by a week. The signed date is the one that matters. If you are not sure which line it is, ask the closing company or your agent to point to it before you book anything.

Book the move so the house is empty before that day, with a spare hour for keys, a last walk, and the utility readings. A truck that arrives on the morning of possession is late if you still have to load it. Give yourself the day before, or the morning before, depending on how much house you have. If the date moves in a written amendment, move the truck with it. A verbal 'we can stay the weekend' is not a new date.

Ask the mover or the rental desk for the price of the day you need, and write that number next to the date. Do not reserve a truck for a day that is not in the contract yet. A reservation deposit is real money, and a date you guessed can cost a change fee. If you need to stay past possession, that is a written change with its own terms, not a favor you mention at the closing table.

The night before possession, the house should already be empty enough that the last hour is for the broom, the keys, and the envelope. If a room is still full that night, you are moving on the wrong day. Look at the calendar again. The contract date does not move because the truck was busy.
steps: Find the possession date and put it on your calendar.
Book the move to finish before that day.
Change the booking only when a written amendment changes the date.
Leave the last hour for keys and a final walk, not for loading.

title: Gather keys and openers in one envelope
summary: Put every key, garage opener, and gate code in one labeled envelope before closing day.
body: A few days before closing, search for every key and opener that operates the house. Check the hooks by the door, the kitchen drawer, the car cup holder, and the coat you wear to the mailbox. House keys, deadbolt keys, mailbox keys, garage door openers, gate remotes, and shed keys all go in one pile. Buyers expect the pieces that make the house work, not a promise that a spare is somewhere in a box.

A standard house-key copy at a hardware store is usually a few dollars. Make the copies you are missing before closing week, while you still have a working original. A garage remote is a different purchase. If one is missing, look again before you buy a replacement, because a new remote can cost much more than a key and may need programming. Write down how many openers you are handing over so the count is not a surprise at the table.

Put the pile in one envelope and label it with the property address. Slide a card inside with gate codes, alarm codes, and the garage keypad code if you use one. Keep a copy of that card in your closing folder until the sale is recorded, then destroy the copy you do not need. Do not pack the envelope in a moving box. Carry it in the same folder as your identification.

On closing morning, count the keys against your card. An example: two house keys, one mailbox key, two garage openers. If a count is short, you still have time to check the car. An envelope you packed at dawn in a carton labeled HALL is the one you will not find when someone asks for the mailbox key.
steps: Search hooks, drawers, and the car for keys and openers.
Copy a missing house key while you still have the original.
Label one envelope with the address and put codes on a card inside.
Carry the envelope to closing instead of packing it.

title: Check your name against your ID
summary: Read the name on the deed papers and make sure it matches the identification you will bring.
body: Read the name on the deed papers and compare it with the identification you will bring. A missing middle initial, an old last name, or a shortened first name can stall a signing. Look at the early pages, not only the signature line. The name has to match the identification, and it has to match the way you have been named in the contract if the contract named you. Write down every version you find.

If the names differ, tell the closing office as soon as you notice. Do not wait for the appointment to see if anyone mentions it. Ask what they need in order to sign. If you have a document that connects the two names, such as a court paper or a prior recorded deed, ask whether to bring it. Bring what they ask for, and bring the identification itself, not a photo of it, unless they have told you a copy is enough.

Put that identification with the envelope of keys and the closing folder so it is not still in a drawer on closing morning. If two people are signing, each person checks their own name and packs their own identification. One person being ready does not clear the other. Read both names even if only one of you has been on the phone with the closing office.

Check the statement and the deed against each other once the statement arrives. A name corrected on one document and not the other is still a mismatch. If you have recently changed how you sign, practice is not the issue. The printed name is the issue. Arrive with the papers, the identification, and the note of what the office told you to bring. A stall at the table is a poor time to learn the requirement.
steps: Read the name on the deed papers and on the contract.
Compare it with the identification you will bring.
Tell the closing office if the names differ, and bring what they ask for.
Pack that identification with the closing folder, for each person who will sign.

title: Leave utility numbers for the final reading
summary: Write the account numbers and schedule the final readings for the possession date.
body: Call each utility and ask for a final reading on the day you give up possession. Write the confirmation number, the date, and the phone number you called. Electric, gas, water, and trash may be four calls, not one. Do them from the account card you are about to make, so you are reading the account number instead of guessing it from a bill in a drawer.

Keep the account numbers on one card in the closing folder. You will want them if a bill arrives after you leave. Include the service address and the last four digits if the full number feels sensitive, but keep enough that you can identify the account when you call. A card in the folder beats a portal login you cannot remember from the new house.

Do not shut a service off early if the contract says the house stays heated or lit until possession. Match the shutoff to the date you already signed. A winter possession with the heat off is a broken pipe you may still be discussing. If the buyer is supposed to start service the same day, ask the utility what happens if there is a gap, and write the answer on the card. You want a handoff, not a dark house.

Leave the card copy, or the confirmation numbers, where the closing file can find them, and take a photo of the card for yourself. If a final bill is wrong, the confirmation number is the first thing the utility will ask for. Schedule the calls a few days before possession so a missed hold time does not land on moving morning. The readings are part of closing, not an errand you do after the truck is loaded.
steps: Call each utility and schedule a final reading for the possession date.
Write the account numbers and the confirmation numbers on one card.
Match any shutoff to the date in the contract, and do not cut heat or lights early.
Keep the card in the closing folder and a copy with you.

title: Measure doors before you book a truck
summary: Measure the sofa, the mattress, and the narrowest doorway before you reserve a truck.
body: A piece that fit on the way in may not fit on the way out if you have added a railing, a new door, or a turn the truck plan skips. Measure before you reserve the truck. Write the height and the width of the largest pieces and of the smallest doorway they must pass, including the landing and the turn, not only the door slab. A sofa that clears the door and dies at the corner still does not leave.

Measure the sofa, the mattress, the table that does not collapse, and any appliance you are taking. Write inches, not about three feet. Then measure the narrowest door, the stair rail, and the path to the truck. Share those numbers with the mover or use them yourself. If the mover asks whether it will fit and you answer it always has, you have skipped the tip. Read them the inches.

If a piece will not pass, decide now whether it stays, gets sold, or needs a different door. Taking a door off the hinges is a plan only if you have the tools and the time, and if the opening without the door is actually wide enough. A screwdriver and a helper are cheaper than a gouge in a jamb you no longer own, or in one you still do. Do not decide on the ramp.

Put the measurements on the same page as the truck reservation. If you are renting by the hour, a piece that has to be winched or left behind changes the hour count. Ask the rental desk what the truck's ramp can take, and write that down too. A reservation without the inches is a guess with a deposit. The inches are the part you can know today, with a tape you already own.
steps: Measure the largest furniture and the narrowest door, including the turn.
Write the inches down and share them with the mover or use them yourself.
Decide now what happens to anything that will not pass.
Put the measurements on the same page as the truck reservation.

title: Pack a first-week kitchen box
summary: Fill one box with the pan, mugs, soap, and towels you will want before the rest is unpacked.
body: Choose one sturdy box and mark it OPEN FIRST on two sides, in the same thick marker you use for the room labels. This box is the one you can live out of before the rest is unpacked. Put in a pan, a knife, mugs, soap, towels, a sponge, and any medicine you take daily. Add a roll of paper towels and a trash bag. The first night fails on small things, not on furniture.

Tape a short list to the top so you do not reopen the box to check what you packed. If it is not on the list, it is not in the box. That rule keeps you from slicing the tape six times. Pack the box the day before, when you can still grab a missing mug from the cupboard. A box packed at midnight is how the can opener stays in a random kitchen box on the truck.

Load that box in your own car, not in the back of the truck. If the truck is late, you can still cook and wash. Set it on the seat or in the trunk where it will not be grabbed by a helper who is trying to be useful. Tell the people loading: this one stays. The closing folder and your identification can sit beside it. You are building the car as the place the essentials live.

At the new place, open this box first and only this box until you have washed, eaten, and found the medicine. Then start on the room labels. If you packed a second open-first box for the bath, mark it the same way and keep it in the car too. Two labeled boxes you can carry are a plan. A dozen boxes marked open me first are the same as none. The list on the lid is what makes this one different.
steps: Pack one sturdy box with a pan, a knife, mugs, soap, towels, and daily medicine.
Tape a list to the lid and mark OPEN FIRST on two sides.
Carry the box in your car, and tell the loaders it stays there.
Open that box first, and leave the other boxes until you have used it.

title: Forward the mail before you leave
summary: File the mail forward in time for it to start on your possession date.
body: File the mail forward before moving week, not on the morning you leave. The post office needs a start date. Use the possession date in your contract, the day you give up the house, so mail starts going to the new address when you are no longer there to collect it. Filing early also gives you a confirmation to put in the closing folder.

The post office charges a fee for a forward. Ask for the current price when you file, and keep the receipt with the confirmation. Do not guess the fee from an old move. A forward sends most letter mail. It does not, by itself, change the address on your bank, your insurer, the tax office, or the accounts you pay online. Those each need their own update.

Make a short list of the accounts that will not follow the forward. The closing company, the insurer on the house you are leaving, and anyone who drafts a payment from your account belong on it. An example: if the home insurer still has the old house as the mailing address, a bill or a notice can sit in a forwarded pile for days. Update that address when you cancel or replace the policy, and write the date you did it next to the account name.

After you arrive, check the confirmation once. If a piece of mail you expected does not show up within a couple of weeks, contact the sender directly instead of assuming the forward failed. The forward is a bridge. It is not a new address book.
steps: File the mail forward before moving week, with the possession date as the start.
Ask the current fee and save the receipt with your closing papers.
Update accounts that will not follow the forward.
Check once after you arrive, and contact a sender directly if a piece is missing.

title: Photograph the empty rooms on the last day
summary: Take a photo of each empty room, plus the meter readings, before you lock the door.
body: After the furniture is out, walk the house once with your phone before you lock the door. Photograph each room from the doorway, then step in and photograph the far corner. Include the inside of the refrigerator, the inside of the oven if it is empty, and any scratch, stain, or nail hole you want to remember. These frames are for you and for the closing file. They are not listing photos, and they do not need to be pretty.

Photograph the meter readings in the same hour if you can reach them. A gas meter, an electric meter, and a water meter each get their own frame, close enough to read the numbers. Those pictures answer a later question about the final bill without a debate about memory. If a meter is in a locked closet, take the photo when you still have the key, not from the curb after you have handed the keys over.

A scuff on a hardwood floor is a useful example. If you photograph it in daylight, with a shoe or a coin in the frame for scale, you can tell a small mark from a gouge later. The same idea works for a chip in a counter or a crack in a garage floor. You are recording the house as you left it, not building a case. Store the set with your settlement papers, in a folder named for the property, not only on a camera roll you might clear.

The cost is the time, not a camera. A phone you already own is enough. Plan about twenty to forty minutes for a modest house if you are not rushing. Do this after the truck is loaded and before you drop the keys. If you wait until the next morning, you may not be allowed back in, and the empty-house record is gone.
steps: Photograph each empty room from the doorway and from inside.
Photograph meter readings close enough to read.
Include scratches or chips you want to remember, with something for scale.
Save the set with your settlement papers.

title: Carry the closing papers with you
summary: Keep the signed settlement set in your car, not in a box on the truck.
body: Put the signed settlement set, a copy of the key envelope list, and your identification in one folder. That folder rides with you. It does not go in a box labeled office, and it does not go on the truck. If you need a page while the truck is in transit, you still have it. A box you cannot reach until tonight is not a file.

Build the folder the night before, from the closing folder you have been keeping all along. Pull the signed statement, the deed copies you were given, the inclusion list, the utility card, and the identification. If the office handed you a packet, the packet is the core. Add a pen and the phone number of the closing office on the inside cover. You are not packing the whole history of the house. You are packing the pages you might be asked to show.

Put the folder in the front seat, not under a first-night box you will forget to move. If two people are traveling separately, decide whose car holds it and write that on the top. One folder, one car. A split set is how a page goes missing between driveways. The keys you are not handing over, and any garage remote you still need tonight, can live in the same bag so you are not unlocking the new place with a search.

When you arrive, file the folder before you unpack the kitchen. A drawer or a shelf you name out loud is enough. You will not want to hunt for it under towels after a long day, and you may need the utility card sooner than you think. The first-week box can wait ten minutes. The folder should not. If a page is missing when you file it, you still have time to call while the day is fresh. A week later, the truck is gone and so is the easy answer.
steps: Put the signed papers, the key list, and your identification in one folder.
Add the utility card, the inclusion list, and the closing office number.
Carry the folder in the front seat of one car, not on the truck.
File it before you unpack, and call the same day if a page is missing.
